newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FOCUS-Sri Lanka stocks seen some 20 pct higher in 97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sri Lanka stocks seen some 20 pct higher in 97.

text.p: Sri Lanka stocks, which have already gained four percent year, are expected to register more big gains in 1997 on the back of good corporate growth, securities analysts said on Tuesday.
The Colombo Stock Exchange's all-share index was expected to rise some 20 percent for the year, an average of analysts' predictions indicated. The index ended at 633.28 points on Tuesday, up 26.58.
"A rise in the index in 1997 was kicked off by good last quarter 1996 corporate results," said Panduka Ambanpola, head of research at brokerage Jardine Fleming HNB.
About 40 companies accounting for 60 percent of the total market capitalisation of 110.7 billion rupees registered 16.7 percent corporate growth in the last quarter of 1996.
This compared with negative growth averaging 11 percent in the previous three quarters, largely due to a drought and power cuts between March and August last year, he said.
"We therefore believe a 19 percent earnings per share growth, which can take the all-share index to about 725 points by December 1997, is achievable," Ambanpola said.
A recent survey by the Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post rated Colombo the 10th best performing market in the world so far in 1997.
Growth in 1997 is expected mainly from manufacturing, hotels, food and beverage and plantations stocks.

"The all-share should rise to about 725 points by the end of this year due to the fact it ended 1996 at a virtual three-year low due to poor corporate growth after the drought," said Sarinda Unamboowe, general manager of brokerage John Keells.

The index, which fell to a three-year low of below 600 points in June 1996, ended the year at 606.7 points against 665 at the start of the year. The index reached a peak of 1,378 points on March 1, 1994.
Brokerage CT Smith said in a recent report that the Colombo all share "buttressed by increased net foreign inflows, will reach 800 points by end 1997".
Net foreign inflows to the stock market were 4.2 billion rupees in 1996, down from 5.3 billion rupees in 1995.
Net inflows are 723 million rupees so far this year.
Fund managers said falling fixed income interest rates would also lead to a refocusing on the equity market.

The benchmark 12-month treasury bill rate was at 14.23 percent at last week's auction compared to a 1996 high of 19 percent after the Central Bank said it was determined to maintain a low interest rate regime to help corporate growth and boost the stock market.
"Falling interest rates will compel institutional investors to look at stocks, where there are some good selective buys," said Manjula de Silva, general manager of CTC Egle Fund Management.
But he believed the all-share index, which will be hostage to profit-taking, would not rise beyond 700 points.
"Funds which have been starved of profits for about one year will sell every time the all share rises 10-15 points," he said.
